blocks.text: 4.2.1 Model, Variables, Constraints, Objective

GridCap's planning team has written its selection model three times already: once to try GLOP, once for HiGHS and once for a colleague who wanted SCIP. Each copy drifted from the others. The team now wants one model, written once from the formulation, that any solver can take. That is what MathOpt is for: it is OR-Tools' solver-independent modeling layer. You describe the model in Python, and only at solve time do you name the solver that should work on it.

Sections 1 to 3 used MathOpt without stopping to look at it (lesson 1.1.3 showed the five parts of a program). This lesson goes through each building block in turn: what a model holds, what a variable is, how an expression and a constraint are stored, and how the objective is set. At the end you build GridCap's selection model from its formulation and read it back. GridCap is a fictional utility's portfolio, invented for this course.
A MathOpt Program Builds a Model, Then Hands It to a Solver
The OR-Tools documentation opens MathOpt with a two-variable LP. Adapted from that example (its "basic example" page and the sample `basic_example.py`), here is the problem:
And here is the whole program, in five steps:

from ortools.math_opt.python import mathopt

# 1. A model: an empty, named container. Nothing about any solver yet.
model = mathopt.Model(name="getting_started_lp")

# 2. Variables, each with its bounds (its domain).
x = model.add_variable(lb=-1.0, ub=1.5, name="x")
y = model.add_variable(lb=0.0, ub=1.0, name="y")

# 3. Constraints, each one linear comparison.
model.add_linear_constraint(x + y <= 1.5, name="c")

# 4. The objective, with its sense.
model.maximize(x + 2 * y)

# 5. Solve with a named solver, and check how the solve ended before reading anything.
result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.GLOP)
if result.termination.reason != mathopt.TerminationReason.OPTIMAL:
    raise RuntimeError(f"model failed to solve: {result.termination}")
print("termination:", result.termination.reason.name)
print("objective:", result.objective_value())
print("x =", result.variable_values(x), " y =", result.variable_values(y))

# The same model, untouched, on a second solver: only the SolverType changes.
again = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS)
print("HiGHS:", again.termination.reason.name, again.objective_value())

termination: OPTIMAL
objective: 2.5
x = 0.5  y = 1.0
HiGHS: OPTIMAL 2.5
Everything you import comes from one module, `ortools.math_opt.python.mathopt`. Read the steps as two halves:

items: **Steps 1 to 4 build a model.** `mathopt.Model` is a container for variables, constraints and one objective. It is plain data: building it runs no solver, and nothing in it names one. That is why the last two lines can hand the same object to HiGHS without changing it.

**Step 5 solves it.** `mathopt.solve(model, solver_type)` copies the model into the solver you name, runs it, and returns a `SolveResult`. The solver is the second argument and nothing else. Lesson 4.2.3 is about choosing it.

blocks.text: The `if` after the solve is the habit the OR-Tools samples all share: check the **termination reason** (why the solver stopped) before reading values, because a solve that ended without a plan has no values to read. Lesson 4.2.2 reads every part of the result.
The rest of this lesson takes steps 2, 3 and 4 one at a time.
The Model

The model this lesson builds is GridCap's **project-selection MILP**, the one sections 1 to 3 solved: one yes/no decision per project, each funded project starting at its earliest start year. A MILP (mixed-integer linear program, lesson 1.1.3) is a linear model in which some variables may only take whole-number values.

**Sets.** $`P`$ the candidate projects; $`Y`$ the plan's years; $`M \subseteq P`$ the must-do projects; $`\mathcal{G}`$ the alternative groups, each a set of projects of which at most one may be funded; $`C \subseteq P`$ the child projects, each with a parent project $`p(c)`$.

**Parameters.** $`v_i`$, the NPV of project $`i`$ if it starts at its earliest start ($k); $`c_{i,y}`$, what project $`i`$ spends in year $`y`$ when it starts then ($k, 0 in a year it is not worked); $`B_y`$, the budget of year $`y`$ ($k).
**Variables.** $`x_i \in \{0, 1\}`$ for every $`i \in P`$: 1 if project $`i`$ is funded.
**Objective.**
\max \; \sum_{i \in P} v_i\, x_i
**Constraints.**

Each line of the formulation becomes one MathOpt call: a set becomes a Python loop, a variable with its domain becomes `add_variable`, a labelled row becomes `add_linear_constraint` with that label as its `name`, and the objective becomes `maximize`. The next four sections show each call.
A Variable Is Its Bounds and an Integer Flag, and Its Default Bounds Are Infinite

A MathOpt variable has exactly four properties: a lower bound, an upper bound, an integer flag and a name. Its **domain**, the set of values it may take, follows from them. There are three ways to make one, and they differ only in their defaults:

spend  id=0  lb=0  ub=2500  integer=False
crews  id=1  lb=0  ub=6  integer=True
fund   id=2  lb=0  ub=1  integer=True
poles  id=3  lb=0  ub=40  integer=True

`add_binary_variable` is `add_variable(lb=0, ub=1, is_integer=True)` and nothing more; MathOpt has no separate binary type. `add_integer_variable` sets the flag and leaves the bounds to you. Each variable gets an `id`, its position in creation order, which is how the solver refers to it. The `name` is for people: it shows up in logs and error messages, so give every variable one built from its index (`x_P001`), as the formulation's subscripts are.
The value `add_variable` returns is a handle into the model, not a number. Its bounds can be read and changed after it is created, which is the simplest way to fix a decision:

fund.lower_bound = 1                       # now fund = 1: the decision is fixed
print("fund fixed:", fund.lower_bound, "<= fund <=", fund.upper_bound)
fund fixed: 1.0 <= fund <= 1.0

Now the trap. With no bounds given, `add_variable` makes a variable that may take **any** real value, $`-\infty < \text{level} < +\infty`$. Forget the bounds on a quantity that should be non-negative, and the model allows negative spend, negative crews, or, as here, a value that grows without limit:

free = mathopt.Model(name="forgot-the-bounds")
level = free.add_variable(name="level")
print("default bounds:", level.lower_bound, level.upper_bound, "integer:", level.integer)
free.maximize(level)
for solver in (mathopt.SolverType.GLOP, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS):
    print(f"{solver.name}: {mathopt.solve(free, solver).termination.reason.name}")

default bounds: -inf inf integer: False
GLOP: INFEASIBLE_OR_UNBOUNDED
HIGHS: UNBOUNDED

A model is **unbounded** when its objective can be made as good as you like; a real plan never is, so this status always means a missing bound or row. GLOP could only tell that the model was infeasible *or* unbounded; HiGHS said which. Lesson 4.2.2 lists every status. The cure is in the formulation: every variable is written with its domain ($`0 \le s_y \le \bar s`$), and the code passes that domain as `lb` and `ub`, every time.
An Expression Is Built With + and *, and Read Back by Flattening It
A **linear expression** is a sum of number × variable terms plus a constant, such as $`3x + 3y + 5`$. In MathOpt you write it with Python's own `+` and `*`, and the result is an object, not a number:

expr = 2 * x + 3 * y + x + 5
print(type(expr).__name__, "->", expr)

flat = mathopt.as_flat_linear_expression(expr)
print(type(flat).__name__, "offset", flat.offset, {v.name: c for v, c in flat.terms.items()})

print("value at x=1, y=0.5:", mathopt.evaluate_expression(expr, {x: 1, y: 0.5}))
Three things happened:

items: **`+` and `*` build a tree.** `2 * x + 3 * y + x + 5` is stored as a `LinearSum` of its pieces, not added up. MathOpt's source explains why: adding as you go would copy the growing expression at every `+`, so it defers the work until the expression is used.

**Flattening adds it up.** `as_flat_linear_expression` returns a `LinearExpression`: one coefficient per variable (the two `x` terms merged into $`3x`$) and a constant `offset`. You rarely call it yourself; `add_linear_constraint` and `maximize` do it for you.

**`evaluate_expression` computes the value** for given variable values, without a solver: here $`3 \cdot 1 + 3 \cdot 0.5 + 5 = 9.5`$. It is how a test checks what a plan costs under the model's own expressions.

blocks.text: For sums over a set, Python's `sum` works, and MathOpt also offers `mathopt.fast_sum`:

total = sum([x, y, z])                  # Python's sum: a nested LinearSum per addition, starting at 0
quick = mathopt.fast_sum([x, y, z])     # one flat LinearSum over the whole iterable
print("sum:", total, "| fast_sum:", quick)

Both give the same expression. The difference is the tree behind it: `sum` adds one item at a time, so a sum over 10,000 projects nests 10,000 `LinearSum` objects, while `fast_sum` stores the items in one. The `LinearSum` docstring recommends the flat form for large sums, several OR-Tools samples (`facility_location.py`, `writing_seminar.py`) use `fast_sum` for their sums over sets, and this module's `selection.py` does too.
A Constraint Is One Comparison, Stored as lb ≤ expression ≤ ub
`add_linear_constraint` takes one comparison of linear expressions. Whatever form you write, MathOpt moves every variable to the left, every constant to the right, and stores the row as
\text{lb} \;\le\; \sum_j a_j\, x_j \;\le\; \text{ub}
with $`\text{lb} = -\infty`$ or $`\text{ub} = +\infty`$ for a one-sided row. The program builds one row of each form and prints what was stored:

def show(row: mathopt.LinearConstraint) -> None:
    terms = ", ".join(f"{t.coefficient:g}*{t.variable.name}" for t in row.terms())
    print(f"{row.name:8} lb={row.lower_bound:<5g} ub={row.upper_bound:<5g} terms: {terms}")


show(model.add_linear_constraint(x + y <= 1.5, name="upper"))
show(model.add_linear_constraint(x + z >= 1, name="lower"))
show(model.add_linear_constraint(y == 2 * x, name="equal"))
show(model.add_linear_constraint((1 <= y + z) <= 3, name="ranged"))
show(model.add_linear_constraint(2 * x + 5 <= y + 7, name="moved"))
show(model.add_linear_constraint(lb=1, ub=3, expr=x + z, name="keyword"))

upper    lb=-inf  ub=1.5   terms: 1*x, 1*y
lower    lb=1     ub=inf   terms: 1*x, 1*z
equal    lb=0     ub=0     terms: 1*y, -2*x
ranged   lb=1     ub=3     terms: 1*y, 1*z
moved    lb=-inf  ub=2     terms: 2*x, -1*y
keyword  lb=1     ub=3     terms: 1*x, 1*z
Row by row:

items: **`<=` and `>=`** give a row with one infinite bound.
**`==`** gives a row with $`\text{lb} = \text{ub}`$. $`y = 2x`$ became $`y - 2x = 0`$: the variables moved left, so the bounds are both 0.
**A ranged row**, $`1 \le y + z \le 3`$, is one row with both bounds finite, not two rows. Write it with parentheses, `(1 <= y + z) <= 3`, for the reason below.
**Constants on both sides** are moved: $`2x + 5 \le y + 7`$ was stored as $`2x - y \le 2`$.
**The keyword form** `add_linear_constraint(lb=..., ub=..., expr=...)` states the bounds directly. It is handy when the bounds come from data.

blocks.text: Two comparisons are refused, each with a `TypeError` at the line that writes them:

TypeError: __bool__ is unsupported for LowerBoundedExpression
TypeError: If you were trying to create a two-sided or ranged linear inequality of the form `lb <= expr <= ub`, try `(lb <= expr) <= ub` instead
TypeError: != constraints are not supported

Python evaluates `a <= b <= c` as `(a <= b) and (b <= c)`, and the `and` asks the first half whether it is true. A MathOpt comparison is a row, not a truth value, so it refuses; without that refusal the first half would be silently dropped. Hence the parentheses. And `!=` is not a linear row at all: "$`x + y \ne 1`$" cuts the feasible region in two, which no single $`\text{lb} \le \cdot \le \text{ub}`$ can describe. Section 6 shows how a binary variable states such an either-or rule.

The `show` function above read the row back through the handle `add_linear_constraint` returned: its `name`, `lower_bound`, `upper_bound` and `terms()`, each term a `variable` and a `coefficient`. Those are also the bounds and coefficients you can change later (lesson 4.3.4 re-solves after such edits).
The Objective Is Set by maximize or minimize, and a Second Call Replaces the First
A model has one objective, `model.objective`. `maximize(expr)` and `minimize(expr)` set its expression and its sense in one call, and calling either again replaces both:

model.maximize(2 * x + y)
print("first :", model.objective.is_maximize, dict(sorted((t.variable.name, t.coefficient) for t in model.objective.linear_terms())))
model.minimize(x - y + 10)
print("second:", model.objective.is_maximize, dict(sorted((t.variable.name, t.coefficient) for t in model.objective.linear_terms())),
      "offset", model.objective.offset)

result = mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS)
print(result.termination.reason.name, "objective", result.objective_value(),
      "x =", result.variable_values(x), "y =", result.variable_values(y))

The second call did not add to the first; the model now minimizes $`x - y + 10`$ and the first objective is gone. The constant 10 is kept as the objective's **offset**, and the reported objective value includes it: $`0 - 1.5 + 10 = 8.5`$. A constant cannot change which plan is best, but it makes the reported number mean something, such as a fixed cost every plan pays.

Two consequences for real code. Build the objective as one expression (with `fast_sum` over the set) and set it once; an objective assembled by several `maximize` calls keeps only the last. And check the sense: maximizing a cost or minimizing a value is a model that solves happily and answers the wrong question. Lesson 4.3.2 adds *auxiliary* objectives for ranked goals; the main objective still works as shown here.

Build From the Formulation One Labelled Row at a Time, and Read the Model Back
`selection.py` turns the formulation of The Model into code, one block per line of it. The variables first, one per project, with their domain:

x = {p.project_id: model.add_variable(lb=0, ub=1, is_integer=integer, name=f"x_{p.project_id}")
         for p in portfolio.projects}
Then each family of rows, under its quantifier, named after its label:

The `x` dict, keyed by project id, is the formulation's subscript: $`x_i`$ is `x["P001"]`. The budget rows are kept in a dict by year too, because later lessons read their dual values. The `integer` argument is the only difference between the MILP and its LP relaxation.
After building, read the model back to check it says what the formulation says. Counting rows by label and reading one row's terms catches most building mistakes before any solve:

rows = list(model.linear_constraints())
kinds = {}
for row in rows:
    label = row.name.split("_")[0]
    kinds[label] = kinds.get(label, 0) + 1
print(f"{model.name}: {model.get_num_variables()} variables, {model.get_num_linear_constraints()} rows {kinds}")
x = sel.x["P001"]
print(f"{x.name}: lb={x.lower_bound:g} ub={x.upper_bound:g} integer={x.integer}")

row = sel.budget[2027]
terms = sorted(((t.variable.name, t.coefficient) for t in row.terms()), key=lambda t: -t[1])
print(f"{row.name}: {len(terms)} terms, ub={row.upper_bound:,.0f}; largest: {terms[:3]}")

objective = model.objective
print("maximize:", objective.is_maximize, "| terms:", len(list(objective.linear_terms())),
      "| offset:", objective.offset)

GridCap small-selection: 40 variables, 13 rows {'must': 4, 'alt': 2, 'needs': 2, 'budget': 5}
x_P001: lb=0 ub=1 integer=True
budget_2027: 10 terms, ub=8,890; largest: [('x_P032', 5680.0), ('x_P034', 2130.0), ('x_P036', 1870.0)]
maximize: True | terms: 40 | offset: 0.0
OPTIMAL NPV 22,532k, 25 projects funded

Forty projects give 40 binaries; 4 must-dos, 2 alternative groups, 2 child projects and 5 years give 13 rows. The 2027 budget row has 10 terms, not 40: a project that spends nothing in 2027 gets a coefficient of 0, and MathOpt stores no zero coefficients. The last line is the solve, with HiGHS, of the model as built.
Names are for people, but MathOpt does check them, and not when you would expect. Two variables with the same name are accepted when you create them and refused when you solve:

model = mathopt.Model(name="duplicate-names")
first = model.add_binary_variable(name="x_P001")
second = model.add_binary_variable(name="x_P001")      # accepted here: nothing is checked yet
model.maximize(first + second)
print("built:", model.get_num_variables(), "variables, both named", first.name)
try:
    mathopt.solve(model, mathopt.SolverType.HIGHS)
except Exception as error:                              # OR-Tools 9.15 raises an AttributeError here
    print("raised:", type(error).__name__)
    print("reason:", error.__context__)                # the real message (lesson 4.2.4)

built: 2 variables, both named x_P001
raised: AttributeError
reason: duplicate name inserted: x_P001; ModelProto.variables are invalid [INVALID_ARGUMENT]

The docstring of `add_variable` says it: names are for debugging, "but nonempty names must be distinct". The check runs when `solve` exports the model, so a loop that builds a name from the wrong index (two projects named `x_2027`) fails there, far from the line that caused it. The exception is also not the one MathOpt meant to raise: in OR-Tools 9.15 the reason is hidden behind an `AttributeError`, and lesson 4.2.4 shows how to read it.
<!-- practice 2 -->
Summary

items: **A MathOpt program builds a model, then hands it to a solver.** The model names no solver; `mathopt.solve(model, solver_type)` does, and its termination reason is checked before anything is read.

**A variable is its bounds and an integer flag.** `add_binary_variable` is bounds 0 and 1 with the flag; `add_variable` with no bounds is free in both directions, so always pass the formulation's domain.
**An expression is built with `+` and `*`** and kept as a tree; `as_flat_linear_expression` adds it up, `evaluate_expression` computes its value, and `fast_sum` keeps a large sum flat.
**A constraint is one comparison, stored as lb ≤ expression ≤ ub.** A ranged row needs parentheses; `!=` is refused.
**The objective is set by `maximize` or `minimize`,** and a second call replaces the first; a constant becomes its offset.
**Build from the formulation one labelled row at a time, and read the model back.** Duplicate names are refused at solve time.

Challenges

items: Write the GridCap budget row with the keyword form, `add_linear_constraint(lb=..., ub=..., expr=...)`. What value do you give `lb`?
Add a variable for unspent money in each year, $`u_y \ge 0`$, and change each budget row to an equation. Read one row back: what are its bounds now?
Build the selection model with `sum` instead of `fast_sum` on the large portfolio and time both builds. Is the difference worth a line of code?

blocks.text: Design Note: Keep the Model Builder Free of Solver Choices

`selection.build` returns a model and the handles to its variables and rows; it never solves, never sets a parameter and never names a solver. That separation is what MathOpt is designed around, and it pays off in three ways. Tests can build the model and inspect it without a solver (the read-back above). The same builder serves the LP relaxation and the MILP. And the solver can change, in a config file or a command-line flag, without touching the model, which is how several OR-Tools samples take their solver: as a flag whose value is a `SolverType`. Lesson 4.2.3 does exactly that.
